title: Addiction
situation: I keep going back to the thing that is destroying me.

echo.heading: The Blind Man at Bethsaida
echo.text: When they arrived at Bethsaida, some people brought a blind man and begged Jesus to touch him. So He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. Then He spit on the man’s eyes and placed His hands on him. “Can you see anything?” He asked. The man looked up and said, “I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.” Once again Jesus placed His hands on the man’s eyes, and when he opened them his sight was restored, and he could see everything clearly. Jesus sent him home and said, “Do not go back into the village.”
echo.situation: A person seeks help for a persistent problem that requires gradual healing rather than an immediate fix.
echo.context: In Bethsaida, Jesus takes a blind man by the hand and leads him out of the village to heal him in private. After an initial partial restoration of sight where the man sees people like trees, Jesus lays hands on him a second time, fully restoring his vision before sending him home without returning to the village.
echo.connection: This gradual healing may echo the non-linear process of breaking cycles of addiction, where recovery often requires repeated intervention rather than a single moment of change. The instruction not to return to the village can resemble the need to step away from environments that trigger destructive patterns while navigating the difficult path toward clarity.

promise.heading: The Prophet’s Hope
promise.text: Remember my affliction and wandering, the wormwood and the gall. Surely my soul remembers and is humbled within me. Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness! “The LORD is my portion,” says my soul, “therefore I will hope in Him.” The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him. It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD. It is good for a man to bear the yoke while he is still young. Let him sit alone in silence, for the LORD has laid it upon him. Let him bury his face in the dust— perhaps there is still hope. Let him offer his cheek to the one who would strike him; let him be filled with reproach. For the Lord will not cast us off forever. Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion. For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men. To crush underfoot all the prisoners of the land, to deny a man justice before the Most High, to subvert a man in his lawsuit— of these the Lord does not approve.
promise.situation: A person endures deep suffering and humiliation while finding strength to hope in enduring kindness that renews daily.
promise.context: The speaker, likely Jeremiah in Jerusalem after its destruction, reflects on personal affliction and national ruin while choosing to remember God's steadfast love as a source of hope amidst despair.
promise.connection: This passage may echo the experience of someone trapped in a cycle of addiction by acknowledging the pain of relapse while offering a tentative glimpse of renewal through daily mercy rather than immediate resolution.

prayer.heading: Out of the Depths
prayer.text: Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD! O Lord, hear my voice; let Your ears be attentive to my plea for mercy. If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared. I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope. My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning— more than watchmen wait for the morning. O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance. And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.
